messages.subject: ddply / count puzzle
parts:
I expected the results of count to be like those of summarize with length, as
shown below.

I also figured that with ddply there were bound to be only 3 rows in the
output, one for each id. But ddply with count gives 4 rows.

Could anyone explain to me why ddply(...count) works as it does below?
> d

id x
1 c 1
2 a 2
3 b 3
4 c 4
>
> ddply(d, .(id), count)

id x freq
1 a 2 1
2 b 3 1
3 c 1 1
4 c 4 1
>
> ddply(d, .(id), summarize, n=length(id))

id n
1 a 1
2 b 1
3 c 2

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

messages.author: 373beb702917b8b5
messages.subject: Re: ddply / count puzzle
parts:
On Mon, Jun 3, 2013 at 2:22 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:
> I expected the results of count to be like those of summarize with length, as
> shown below.

Your expectation is wrong. count() counts the numbers in each level of
the 'vars' in 'df', not the length of the 'vars'.

>
> I also figured that with ddply there were bound to be only 3 rows in the
> output, one for each id. But ddply with count gives 4 rows.
>
> Could anyone explain to me why ddply(...count) works as it does below?
>> d
>
> id x
> 1 c 1
> 2 a 2
> 3 b 3
> 4 c 4
>>
>> ddply(d, .(id), count)
>
> id x freq
> 1 a 2 1
> 2 b 3 1
> 3 c 1 1
> 4 c 4 1

The idea behind ddply is that you split up the data.frame based on the
second argument ('id' in your example)) and run .fun (count in your
example) on each part. So let's see what count does with the 'id==c'
slice:

count(subset(d, id=="c"))
id x freq
1 c 1 1
2 c 4 1

Hope this helps, though I'm not confident it will--if not post back
and I'm sure someone else will be able to explain it more elegantly.

Best,
Ista

>>
>> ddply(d, .(id), summarize, n=length(id))
>
> id n
> 1 a 1
> 2 b 1
> 3 c 2
>
> Thanks.
> Ross Boylan

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: ddply / count puzzle
parts:
Hi:

The count() function has two formal arguments: vars and wt_var. The
former indicates which variable(s) is/are to be counted, the latter
the variable(s) whose values are to be counted. Here are some examples
of how it could have been used with these data, which I named DF.

# Your initial call...
ddply(DF, .(id), count)

id x freq
1 a 2 1
2 b 3 1
3 c 1 1
4 c 4 1

id x freq
1 a 2 1
2 b 3 1
3 c 1 1
4 c 4 1

which indicates that the default choice of vars is the variable (or
variables) not among the set of grouping variables. This also
illuminates a feature of the **ply() functions to which Ista alluded:
after the 'apply' function is defined, arguments can be passed to it
in a comma-separated fashion, similar to the apply family functions.
For ddply(), the general structure is

ddply(data_frame, .(grouping_variables), function, <arguments_to_function>)

In particular, for the count() function, you can pass arguments for
vars = and wt_var = .
>

# Your second call is equivalent to
> ddply(DF, .(id), count, vars = "id")
id freq

# which is basically the same as
# as.data.frame(table(DF$id)) using base code.

# This call still uses x as the default vars argument,
# which is why x and freq are the same.
> ddply(DF, .(id), count, wt_var = "x")
id x freq
1 a 2 2
2 b 3 3
3 c 1 1
4 c 4 4

# However, when ID is the default 'count variable' and
# x is the weighting variable, we then get a result which
# is equivalent to sum(x) for each id.
> ddply(DF, .(id), count, vars = "id", wt_var = "x")
id freq
1 a 2
2 b 3
3 c 5

It appears the confusion lies in what count() takes as the default
value for the vars = argument. Hope this clarifies matters somewhat.

Dennis
